title: Communication & Self-Expression
subtitle: Listen well, say what you feel and need, and say no with respect, at home, in the market, at work and in your community.
description: A practical course in everyday interpersonal communication. You will learn how messages get lost, how to listen so people feel heard, how to express feelings and needs without blame using Nonviolent Communication, and how to hold boundaries and handle difficult conversations respectfully. You finish by planning and reflecting on a real conversation from your own life.
outcomes: Trace where a misunderstanding started and choose the right channel for a message
Recognise passive, aggressive, passive-aggressive and assertive styles and rewrite messages assertively
Listen actively using paraphrase, open questions and summaries
Express a feeling, need and clear request using the four steps of Nonviolent Communication
Say no and hold boundaries with the Yes, No, Yes structure, including with elders and seniors
Plan, rehearse and reflect on a real difficult conversation, and track your progress with a journal
audience: Women who want to express themselves clearly and respectfully in family, market, workplace and community situations, with no prior training needed.
tools: A smartphone with a voice recorder and notes app
A notebook and pen for your profile and journal
A trusted friend or family member to practise with

modules.title: Foundations: How You Communicate Today
modules.overview: You will see how a message travels from your mind to another person, where it gets lost, and how to choose the right channel. You will learn to recognise the four communication styles in real talk and in WhatsApp messages, and you will map your own strengths, hard situations and safety limits.

lessons.title: How a message travels: sender, channel, noise and feedback
objectives: Name the six parts of a simple communication model
Find the point where a misunderstanding started
Choose between face to face, phone call, voice note and text for a message
Use a feedback check to confirm you were understood

blocks.text: Many arguments at home, in the market and in meetings do not start with bad intentions. They start with a message that left one person's mind and arrived in a different shape in another person's mind. Communication scholars have drawn simple models of this journey since the middle of the last century. You do not need the theory, but one plain picture helps you find where things went wrong.

blocks.name: conversation
blocks.alt: Two people talking with speech bubbles between them
blocks.caption: Every conversation is a message sent, received and checked, again and again.

blocks.text: The six parts of every message

head: Part
What it means
Market example
rows: Sender
The person with the idea, need or feeling
You, a tomato seller, want to tell a regular buyer that prices went up
Message
What you actually say or write, not what you meant
"Prices have changed, the basket is now more"
Channel
The route: face to face, phone call, voice note, text, letter
A quick shout across the stall
Receiver
The person who hears and interprets it
Your buyer, already rushing to catch a bus
Noise
Anything that blocks or bends the message
Traffic, a crying child, her worry about money, your unclear words
Feedback
The reply that shows what was understood
She frowns and says "You people just increase anyhow"

blocks.text: In the example, the buyer heard "you are cheating me", while you meant "transport costs went up for all of us". The message was vague ("more", but how much?), the channel was rushed, and her money worry was noise. Her angry reply is not the end of the story. It is **feedback**, and feedback is useful because it shows you exactly what arrived.

blocks.title: The communication loop
items: Sender has an idea
Puts it into words
Sends through a channel
Receiver interprets it
Receiver gives feedback
blocks.caption: Noise can enter at every step, so the loop only closes when feedback confirms the meaning.

blocks.text: Two kinds of noise

**Outside noise** is physical: a generator, a weak network that cuts a call, a busy road. **Inside noise** lives in people: tiredness, hunger, fear, old quarrels, assumptions about age or status, or simply thinking about something else. Inside noise is often the bigger problem. A wife who asks her husband about school fees just as he walks in from a hard day meets a lot of inside noise, even in a quiet room.
Choosing the right channel

Every channel carries some parts of a message and drops others. Face to face carries words, tone, face and body. A phone call keeps words and tone but loses the face. A voice note keeps tone but removes the chance to respond at once. A text keeps only the words, so the reader adds her own tone, often a worse one than you intended.

head: Channel
Best for
Weak for
rows: Face to face
Feelings, disagreements, apologies, important requests to elders
Long lists of details people must remember
Phone call
Quick decisions, warm check-ins, sorting confusion fast
Numbers and addresses that need to be kept
Voice note
Warmth when you cannot meet, explaining in your own language
Anything the listener must find again later, or listen to in a noisy place
Text or WhatsApp message
Times, amounts, addresses, confirmations, records
Delicate feelings, anger, bad news

blocks.title: Data and cost
blocks.text: Voice notes and video calls use more data than short texts. If the other person has costly or limited data, a short clear text plus a phone call for the sensitive part can be kinder than a five-minute voice note.
Close the loop with a feedback check

The most useful habit in this lesson is the **feedback check**: after an important message, ask the other person to tell you what they understood, or tell them what you understood. Do it warmly so it does not sound like a test. "Just so I know I explained it well, what will you tell the others?" puts the responsibility on you, not on them.

blocks.title: Worked example: fixing a cooperative meeting time
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi is secretary of a women's savings group of 20 members in Enugu. She sends a WhatsApp message: "Meeting moved to Saturday." Six members come on the wrong day.
steps: She finds the noise: two Saturdays were possible, and three members read the message late at night and only saw the preview.
She rewrites the message with all the facts: "Our meeting is now Saturday 14th, 4pm, at Mama Chidi's shop. Not this coming Saturday. Please reply OK when you see this."
She asks for feedback: replies of "OK" let her count who has seen it. After a day, 17 of 20 have replied.
She calls the 3 who have not replied, because a call reaches people the group chat does not.
blocks.result: All 20 members know the correct date. The fix was not more words, but specific words plus a feedback check: date, time, place, a clear contrast with the wrong date, and a way to confirm.

blocks.text: When a conversation goes wrong, try walking backwards through the loop before you blame anyone. Was the message clear? Was the channel right? What noise was there? What did the feedback tell you? This calm review is the foundation for everything else in this course.

takeaways: A message is what you said, not what you meant
Noise can be outside (sound, network) or inside (worry, assumptions)
Match the channel to the message: feelings face to face, facts in writing
Close the loop with a warm feedback check

activity.title: Trace one misunderstanding
steps: Think of a recent misunderstanding at home, work or in a group chat.
Write the six parts: sender, message, channel, receiver, noise, feedback.
Circle the part where you think the meaning changed.
Rewrite the message the way you would send it now, choosing the best channel.
Add one feedback-check question you could have asked.
activity.evidence: A photo of your handwritten six-part trace and rewritten message

lessons.title: Passive, aggressive, passive-aggressive or assertive: spotting the four styles
objectives: Describe the four communication styles and the belief behind each
Recognise each style in spoken words, body language and WhatsApp messages
Rewrite a passive, aggressive or passive-aggressive message as an assertive one
Explain why assertive does not mean loud or disrespectful

blocks.text: Everyone uses all four styles at different times. A woman can be passive with her mother-in-law, aggressive with her children after a long day, and assertive with customers. The goal of this lesson is not to label people. It is to notice which style you are using in the moment, so you can choose.

blocks.name: agree
blocks.caption: Assertive communication aims for an outcome both people can accept.

blocks.text: The four styles and the belief underneath

head: Style
Hidden belief
Sounds like
Usual result
rows: Passive
Your needs matter, mine do not
"It's fine, no problem" (when it is a problem)
Resentment builds; others do not know what she needs
Aggressive
My needs matter, yours do not
"You are useless, you never do anything right"
People obey or fight back, but trust drops
Passive-aggressive
My needs matter, but I will not say so openly
Silence, sarcasm, "Ehen, do as you like", leaving messages on read
Confusion and hidden conflict
Assertive
Both our needs matter
"I need the money by Friday because my rent is due. Can you manage that?"
Clear requests, respect on both sides

blocks.title: Four styles on two scales
items: Aggressive
Assertive
Passive-aggressive
Passive
axes: Respect for the other person (low to high)
Openness about my needs (low to high)
blocks.caption: Openness plus respect gives assertive; openness without respect gives aggressive; hiding your needs gives passive or passive-aggressive.

blocks.text: A simpler way to remember it: assertive communication is **honest and respectful at the same time**. Passive is respectful but not honest. Aggressive is honest but not respectful. Passive-aggressive is neither: the anger is real, but it leaks out sideways.
Spotting the styles in WhatsApp messages
Text removes tone, so styles show up in word choice, punctuation and timing. Read these replies to a friend who asks to borrow your gele for a wedding and has not returned the last one.

items: Passive: "Ok no wahala 😊" (while you are upset inside).
Aggressive: "YOU ARE NOT SERIOUS. Return my things first before you open your mouth."
Passive-aggressive: "Hmm. Some people sha." or a seen message with no reply for three days.
Assertive: "I'm happy to help, but I need the blue one back first. Can you bring it on Sunday? Then you can take this one."

blocks.text: Notice that the assertive reply is not cold. It keeps the friendship, states the condition and asks a clear question with a time. Capital letters, many exclamation marks and voice notes recorded while angry usually push a message towards aggressive, even when you did not intend it.

blocks.title: Worked example: rewriting a reply to a committee chair
blocks.context: For example, Halima, a trader in Kano, is asked by her church women's committee chair to cook for 80 people at a programme in two days, on top of her shop work. Her first instinct is "Yes ma, no problem" (passive), then to complain to others later (passive-aggressive).
steps: She names the facts: she can cook for about 30 people alone; 80 needs at least three helpers and money for ingredients.
She names her need: she wants to support the programme without losing two days of sales.

She drafts an assertive reply: "Ma, thank you for trusting me with this. I can lead the cooking if two or three women join me and the committee buys the ingredients. Alone, I can manage rice and stew for 30. Which would you prefer?"
She checks it against the four styles: honest about her limit, respectful in tone, gives two clear options, asks a question.
blocks.result: The chair assigns three helpers and releases money for ingredients. Halima keeps her shop open the day before and still serves the programme, and nobody is left guessing what she thought.

blocks.title: Assertive is not the same as loud
blocks.text: In many Nigerian homes and communities, softness, greetings and respect words like "ma" and "sir" are part of good manners. You can keep all of them. Assertiveness lives in what you ask for clearly, not in volume or rudeness. A quiet voice with a clear request is assertive.
Why we slide out of assertiveness

People become passive when they fear conflict, rejection or losing a relationship, or when they were raised to believe that a good woman does not ask. People become aggressive when they are exhausted, feel ignored for too long, or have seen shouting work. Passive-aggressive behaviour often grows where open disagreement feels forbidden. Knowing your own trigger helps: many people notice they slide to aggressive when hungry or tired, and to passive with anyone older or more senior.

items: To move back to assertive in the moment, pause and breathe out slowly before you answer.
Ask yourself two questions: what do I actually need here, and what does the other person need?
Say your need in one sentence, then ask one clear question.
If you are too angry to be respectful, say "Let me answer you later today" and set a time.

blocks.text: In the next lesson you will look honestly at your own patterns, and at the times when speaking up needs extra care.

takeaways: Assertive means honest and respectful at the same time
Passive-aggressive anger leaks out through silence, sarcasm and hints
Text strips tone, so choose words, capitals and timing carefully
Respect words and a soft voice fit perfectly with assertive requests

activity.title: Style spotting in your own chats
steps: Open three recent WhatsApp chats where there was tension or a request.
Copy one message you sent in each chat into your notebook.
Label each one: passive, aggressive, passive-aggressive or assertive.
Rewrite any non-assertive message so it is honest, respectful and ends with a clear question.
Read the rewrites aloud and check they still sound like you.
activity.evidence: Notebook page with three original messages, their labels and your assertive rewrites

lessons.title: Your communication profile and when speaking up is safe
objectives: Rate your comfort across ten common communication situations
Pick one realistic focus situation for this course
Decide whether a situation is a good time, a wait-and-prepare time, or not safe
Know where to turn if speaking up could put you in danger

blocks.text: Before learning new skills, it helps to know your starting point. Most people are confident in some situations and freeze in others. A woman who bargains boldly in the market may go silent when her husband's family discusses money. A nurse who speaks clearly to patients may struggle to disagree with a senior doctor. Your profile shows where practice will make the biggest difference.

blocks.name: shield
blocks.caption: Good communication includes knowing when and how to protect yourself.

blocks.text: Rate yourself honestly
Score each situation from 1 (I avoid it or freeze) to 5 (I handle it calmly and clearly). Do not score how you wish you were. Score what you usually do.

head: Situation
Score 1 to 5
rows: Saying no to a request from a relative
Asking a customer or employer for money owed
Disagreeing with someone older or more senior
Speaking in a group meeting or WhatsApp group
Telling someone you are hurt or upset
Receiving criticism without defending at once
Introducing yourself to strangers
Asking for help when you are struggling
Listening without interrupting when you disagree
Apologising when you were wrong

blocks.text: Your **focus situation** is the one with a low score that also matters most in your life right now. Pick something that comes up often, so you get many chances to practise. Avoid starting with the hardest, highest-risk relationship in your life; build skill first in medium situations.

blocks.title: Worked example: reading a profile
blocks.context: For example, Funmi, a hairdresser in Ibadan, scores herself: saying no to relatives 1, asking for money owed 2, disagreeing with seniors 2, group meetings 4, telling someone she is hurt 2, receiving criticism 3, introducing herself 5, asking for help 2, listening 3, apologising 4. Her total is 28 out of 50.
steps: She looks for the lowest scores: saying no to relatives (1) and asking for money owed (2).
She asks which one costs her most. Customers who "will pay later" owe her about ₦18,000 this month (her own record), which hurts her shop more than the relatives' requests.
She chooses "asking customers for money owed" as her focus situation.
She writes it as a goal she can test: "By the end of this course, I will ask every customer with an unpaid balance for payment within one week, using a prepared sentence."
blocks.result: Funmi has a clear, frequent, medium-risk situation to practise. She will retake the same ten ratings at the end of the course to see her change.

blocks.title: Is now the right time to speak?
items: Am I safe here?
Am I calm enough?
Is the other person ready?
Speak now or plan a time
blocks.caption: If the answer to the first question is no, your plan is safety first, not a conversation.

blocks.text: Good time, wait and prepare, or not safe

items: **Good time:** you are calm, the other person is not rushed or angry, you have privacy if it is personal, and you know your main point.

**Wait and prepare:** you are very angry, the person is drunk, hungry or in front of an audience, or you have not yet worked out what you want. Waiting is not passive if you set a time: "Let us talk about this tomorrow evening."

**Not safe:** the person has hit, threatened, controlled or frightened you before, or you fear they will. In this case, assertiveness scripts are not the right tool and the problem is not your communication.

blocks.title: When speaking up could put you in danger
blocks.text: If someone hurts you, threatens you, controls your money or movement, or makes you afraid, your safety comes first. Do not confront them alone to practise this course. Talk privately to someone you trust, a health worker, a religious leader you trust, a recognised women's support organisation or the police. Keep important phone numbers and documents somewhere safe. You deserve help, and getting help is a strong act of self-expression.
Your rights in a conversation

Assertiveness trainers often list basic rights that help people speak up. You have the right to say no without a long excuse, to change your mind, to say "I don't know" or "I don't understand", to ask for what you want, and to make mistakes and correct them. The other person has exactly the same rights. Remembering this keeps your assertiveness fair: you ask clearly, and you accept that the answer may still be no.
Cultural context is not an excuse to stay silent

Respect for elders, husbands, leaders and in-laws is valued in most Nigerian families and communities, and this course respects that. But respect describes how you speak, not whether you speak. You can kneel or bow, greet properly, use "ma" or "sir", choose a private moment and still say clearly what you need. Many communities also have respected go-betweens, such as an aunt or an elder, who can help carry a difficult message. Using them wisely is a skill, not a weakness.

takeaways: Score what you usually do, not what you wish you did
Choose a frequent, medium-risk focus situation to practise
Waiting with a set time is preparation, not avoidance
If someone frightens or harms you, seek help: safety comes first

activity.title: Build your communication profile
steps: Copy the ten-situation table into your notebook and score yourself honestly.
Add up your total out of 50 and write today's date.
Circle your two lowest scores and choose one focus situation.
Write your focus situation as a goal you can check, like Funmi's.
Write the name of one trusted person you could talk to if a situation ever felt unsafe.
activity.evidence: Dated profile table with your total, chosen focus situation and goal

quiz.q: Ada texts her sister "Bring the thing tomorrow". Her sister brings the wrong item. Using the communication loop, where did the problem most likely start?
options: The channel, because texts are never allowed for family
The message, because "the thing" was not specific
The feedback, because her sister replied
The receiver, because her sister is careless
quiz.explain: The words were vague. A specific message (which item, what time) plus a feedback check would have prevented the mistake.

quiz.q: Which channel is usually best for apologising to an elder you upset?
options: Face to face, at a calm and private moment
A long voice note sent late at night
quiz.explain: Apologies and feelings need tone, face and body language, which face-to-face conversation carries best, and privacy shows respect.

quiz.q: A friend has not returned your wrapper. You reply to her new request: "Hmm. Some people sha." Which style is this?
quiz.explain: The annoyance is real but expressed indirectly through a hint, which is passive-aggressive.

quiz.q: Which reply is assertive?
options: "It's fine, no problem" while upset inside
"I can help, but I need the first one back. Can you bring it on Sunday?"
quiz.explain: It is honest about the condition, respectful, and ends with a clear request and time.

quiz.q: Bisi's husband has shouted at and pushed her before when she disagreed. What does this course advise?
options: Practise the assertive scripts on him first
Put safety first and talk privately to someone she trusts or a support organisation
Argue with him in front of the children so there are witnesses
quiz.explain: When someone has harmed or threatened you, the issue is safety, not communication skill. Seek help from trusted people or organisations.

quiz.q: Which is the best focus situation to start practising?
options: The most dangerous relationship in your life
Something that happens often and matters, with medium risk
Something that happens once every five years
A situation you already score 5 in
quiz.explain: Frequent, meaningful, medium-risk situations give you many safe chances to practise and improve.

modules.title: Guided Practice: Listening, Expressing and Saying No
modules.overview: Now you practise the three core moves of self-expression. You will listen so people feel truly heard, express a feeling and a need without blame using the four steps of Nonviolent Communication, and say no to requests while protecting the relationship.

lessons.title: Active listening: paraphrase, clarify and summarise
objectives: Show attention with your body, voice and short encouragers
Paraphrase what someone said so they can confirm or correct it
Ask open questions that help the speaker explain more
Avoid the five common listening blockers

blocks.text: Self-expression is only half of communication. People are far more willing to hear your view after they feel you have heard theirs. **Active listening** means listening to understand the other person's meaning and feelings, and showing them that you understood. It is active because you do something: you attend, reflect, ask and summarise, instead of waiting quietly for your turn to speak.

blocks.name: listening
blocks.caption: Active listening means showing the speaker that her meaning arrived.

blocks.text: The four moves of active listening

blocks.title: Active listening in four moves
items: Attend fully
Paraphrase the meaning
Ask open questions
Summarise and check
blocks.caption: Each move gives the speaker a chance to confirm or correct what you understood.

items: **Attend.** Put the phone face down, turn towards the person, and use small encouragers: a nod, "mm", "I see", "go on". In many cultures steady eye contact with an elder can feel disrespectful, so soft, occasional eye contact with a respectful posture is fine.
**Paraphrase.** Say back the main point in your own words: "So the supplier delivered late twice, and now you are worried about your Christmas orders." You are not agreeing yet; you are checking.

**Ask open questions.** Open questions start with what, how, which or tell me, and invite a full answer: "What worries you most about it?" Closed questions get yes or no and are useful only for checking facts: "Was it on Tuesday?"

**Summarise.** At the end, pull the main points together and check: "Let me be sure I have it: three things, the late delivery, the cost, and that you don't want to lose this customer. Did I miss anything?"

blocks.text: Reflecting feelings, not only facts

Good listeners also notice the feeling under the words and name it gently, as a question: "You sound really tired of this. Is that right?" If you guess wrong, the speaker will correct you, and that is fine; the correction still helps her feel understood. Avoid telling people what they feel as if you know: "You are just jealous" is a judgement, not a reflection.
Five listening blockers

head: Blocker
What it sounds like
Try instead
rows: Interrupting
"Wait, wait, let me tell you..."
Let her finish, then paraphrase
Fixing too fast
"Just leave him. Next!"
"What options are you thinking about?"
Story-stealing
"That is nothing, my own case was worse..."
Stay with her story for now
Mind-reading
"I know what you are going to say"
Ask: "What happened next?"
Rehearsing
Planning your reply while she is still talking
Listen for the words you will paraphrase

blocks.title: Worked example: a teenage daughter and a school problem
blocks.context: For example, Grace, a mother in Port Harcourt, notices her 15-year-old daughter Ebi is quiet after school. Her old habit was to ask "What is wrong with you?" and then lecture.
steps: Attend: Grace waits until dinner is finished, sits beside Ebi and says, "You've been quiet today. I'm here if you want to talk."
Ebi says some girls laughed at her answer in class. Grace paraphrases: "So you answered a question and some girls laughed at you."
She reflects the feeling as a question: "That sounds embarrassing. Is that how it felt?" Ebi nods and adds that it happens often.
She asks an open question instead of fixing: "What would help you most right now?"
She summarises: "So it happens often, it makes you not want to answer in class, and you want me to know but not to go to the school yet. Have I got it?"
blocks.result: Ebi talks for ten minutes, which is longer than usual. Grace learns it is a repeated pattern, and they agree to talk again on Friday and decide together whether to speak to the class teacher.

blocks.text: Listening when you disagree

Active listening is hardest when you strongly disagree, and that is exactly when it is most useful. Understanding is not the same as agreeing. You can say, "So your view is that the levy should rise to ₦2,000 because the hall rent went up. I see it differently, but let me first check I have your reasons right." The other person relaxes because she feels heard, and she is then far more likely to listen to your reasons in return. A simple rule many groups use: before you reply, summarise the last speaker's point to her satisfaction.

blocks.title: Listening on WhatsApp
blocks.text: Active listening works in text too. Before replying to a long or emotional message, quote the key line and paraphrase it: "You said the payment hasn't come since March. Is that right?" This prevents arguing about the wrong problem.

Practise these moves in low-stakes conversations first, such as a friend telling you about her day. After a week the moves start to feel natural, and you will be ready to use them in harder talks. In the next lesson you will learn the other side: expressing your own feelings and needs so others can listen to you.

takeaways: Listen to understand, then show what you understood
Paraphrase and summarise so the speaker can correct you
Open questions start with what, how, which or tell me
Name feelings as a gentle question, not a judgement

activity.title: Two listening conversations
steps: Choose two people to listen to this week, one at home and one outside.
In each conversation, use at least one paraphrase, one open question and one summary.
Notice which blocker you were most tempted to use.
After each conversation, write two sentences about what you learned that you would have missed by interrupting.
activity.evidence: A short note for each conversation: the paraphrase you used, the open question, the blocker you resisted and what you learned

lessons.title: Saying what you feel and need: the four steps of Nonviolent Communication
objectives: Separate an observation from a judgement
Name a real feeling instead of an accusation disguised as a feeling
Connect your feeling to a need
Make a clear, doable request rather than a demand

blocks.text: Many of us were taught to hide feelings or to express them as blame: "You don't respect me", "You people never care". Blame makes the listener defend herself, so your real need gets lost. The psychologist Marshall Rosenberg developed a method called **Nonviolent Communication (NVC)**, described in his book *Nonviolent Communication: A Language of Life*. Its four steps help you say difficult things in a way people can actually hear.

blocks.name: speaking-head-in-silhouette
blocks.caption: NVC gives your words a clear order: what happened, how you feel, what you need, what you ask.

blocks.title: The four NVC steps
items: Observation: what happened
Feeling: how I feel
Need: what matters to me
Request: what I ask
blocks.caption: Say them in this order, in your own natural words.

blocks.text: Step 1: observation, not judgement

An observation is what a video camera would record. A judgement adds your interpretation. "You are lazy" is a judgement. "The plates from last night were still in the sink this morning" is an observation. Words like always, never, lazy, selfish and careless almost always signal judgement. Observations are harder to argue with, so the conversation moves forward.

head: Judgement
Observation
rows: "You never help me in the shop"
"This month you came to the shop on two of the four Saturdays you promised"
"You disrespected me in the meeting"
"When I started to speak in the meeting, you said 'sit down, we have heard enough'"
"That customer is a cheat"
"She took the shoes on 2 March and has not paid the ₦9,500 balance she promised for 9 March"

blocks.text: Step 2: a real feeling

A feeling describes what is happening inside you: worried, hurt, tired, frustrated, embarrassed, disappointed, relieved, grateful. Be careful with words that sound like feelings but really accuse the other person, such as ignored, betrayed, used, cheated or disrespected. They describe what you think someone did to you. "I feel ignored" invites argument; "I feel lonely and hurt" invites care. A useful test: if the sentence still makes sense as "I feel that you...", it is probably a thought, not a feeling.
Step 3: the need underneath

Every feeling points to a need that matters to you: rest, respect, fairness, support, safety, reliability, recognition, honesty, money to meet obligations. Naming the need moves attention from the other person's fault to what you both can protect. "I feel worried because I need to pay the rent on Friday" is very different from "You are making me worried".
Step 4: a request, not a demand

A request is specific, positive and doable now: who will do what, by when. "Please be more responsible" is too vague. "Would you be willing to come to the shop by 9am this Saturday?" is clear. Rosenberg's test for a real request is how you respond to a no. If a no leads to punishment or blame, it was a demand. If you are willing to hear the no and keep talking, it is a request, and people are much more likely to say yes.

blocks.title: Worked example: a sister and a family contribution
blocks.context: For example, Amaka, a teacher in Onitsha, agreed with her three siblings that each would send ₦20,000 a month for their mother's upkeep. Her younger brother Obi has not sent his share for two months. Her first draft: "Obi you are so selfish. You leave everything to me as usual."
steps: Observation: "Obi, for August and September, I didn't see your ₦20,000 for Mama in the family account."
Feeling: "I feel worried and a bit tired,"
Need: "because I want Mama to have what she needs, and I need us to share this fairly as we agreed."
Request: "Would you be willing to tell me by Sunday what you can send this month, even if it's less?"
She checks the numbers: two missed months is ₦40,000 owed, but she asks first about this month, so the conversation can start rather than stall.
blocks.result: Obi replies that he lost a contract in August and can send ₦10,000 now and the rest in November. Amaka learns the real reason, and the agreement is renewed instead of the siblings falling out.

blocks.title: Make it sound like you
blocks.text: NVC can sound stiff if you copy it word for word. Keep the four parts but use your normal words, language and greetings. In Pidgin, Yoruba, Igbo or Hausa the same structure works: what happened, how you feel, what you need, what you are asking.

NVC is also a listening tool. When someone attacks you with blame, you can silently translate their words into the four parts: what did they observe, what might they feel, what might they need? Then you can respond to the need instead of the attack: "It sounds like you are frustrated because you need the order on time. Is that it?"

takeaways: Observations describe what a camera would see
Words like ignored or betrayed are accusations, not feelings
Every feeling points to a need
A real request can accept a no

activity.title: Turn one complaint into an NVC message
steps: Write down one complaint you have been carrying, exactly as you would normally say it.
Underline every judgement word (always, never, lazy, selfish, careless).
Rewrite it in four lines: observation, feeling, need, request.
Read it aloud in your own language and adjust the words until it sounds natural.
If it is safe and the timing is right, use it this week and note the reply.
activity.evidence: Your original complaint and your four-line NVC version, plus a note of the response if you used it

lessons.title: Saying no and holding boundaries without breaking relationships
objectives: Use the Yes, No, Yes structure to refuse a request
Hold your position under pressure with fogging and repeated calm statements
Offer a real alternative when you want to help in a different way
Say no to elders and seniors respectfully

blocks.text: A **boundary** is a limit you set about what you will and will not do, give or accept. Boundaries protect your time, money, body and peace so you can keep giving where it matters. Many women find no the hardest word in any language, because saying yes has been rewarded all their lives. Yet every yes you give unwillingly is a no to something else: your children, your rest, your savings or your business.

blocks.name: my-answer
blocks.alt: A person giving a clear answer
blocks.caption: A clear, kind no is better than an unwilling yes that turns into resentment.

blocks.text: The Yes, No, Yes structure

The negotiation expert William Ury, in his book *The Power of a Positive No*, describes a respectful no in three parts. First, a **yes** to what matters to you (your reason or value). Second, a clear **no**. Third, a **yes?**: an offer or question that keeps the relationship open.

blocks.title: A positive no
items: Yes: my reason
No: clear refusal
Yes?: an alternative
blocks.caption: The first yes explains, the no is short and clear, and the final yes keeps the door open.

blocks.title: Worked example: a loan request from a cousin
blocks.context: For example, Zainab runs a small provisions shop in Kaduna. Her cousin asks to borrow ₦150,000, about the value of most of her shop stock. He did not repay ₦30,000 he borrowed last year.
steps: Yes (her reason): "I'm keeping all my money in the shop this year because I'm building stock for my children's school fees."
No (short and clear): "So I can't lend you the ₦150,000."
Yes? (an alternative she is truly willing to give): "What I can do is ask my supplier if he needs a sales boy, or help you write to the cooperative about their loan."
She does not mention the old ₦30,000 here, because her no does not depend on it. She can raise it separately, as its own conversation.
blocks.result: The cousin is disappointed but not insulted. Zainab's stock stays intact, and he accepts her offer to ask the supplier about work.

blocks.text: Staying firm under pressure

Often the first no is not accepted. The other person repeats the request, adds guilt or brings in others. Two techniques from the assertiveness book *When I Say No, I Feel Guilty* by Manuel J. Smith help you stay calm.

items: **Calm repetition** (Smith calls it the broken record): repeat your main sentence in the same calm tone, without new excuses. "I understand. I still can't lend the money." Each new excuse gives the other person something to argue with.

**Fogging:** agree with any part of the criticism that is true, without changing your decision. "You're right, I did help Ifeoma last year. I still can't do it this time." There is nothing left to fight about.
**Ask for time:** you do not have to answer on the spot. "Let me think about it and tell you tomorrow" protects you from saying yes under pressure.

blocks.title: Do not over-explain
blocks.text: Long explanations sound like an invitation to negotiate. One honest reason is enough. You do not owe anyone a list of your expenses or your bank balance to justify a no.
Saying no up the ladder

With a parent, in-law, pastor, imam, boss or community leader, keep the structure but add respect: greet properly, thank them for thinking of you, choose a private moment, and offer a real alternative. "Ma, thank you for asking me. This month I am already committed to my shop every evening, so I can't lead the visitation team. I can bring drinks for the team on Sunday, if that would help." You have still said no, clearly.

head: Situation
A respectful no
rows: Boss asks for unpaid weekend work again
"I've worked the last two Saturdays. I can't this weekend. I can stay an hour late on Thursday to finish the report."
Friend wants you to hold goods you can't store
"I'd like to help, but my room is full and I can't keep your bags. Shall I ask the woman next door who has a store?"
Relative wants to stay with you for three months
"You are welcome for a week while you find a place. After that I can't host you, but I'll help you look."

blocks.text: Expect to feel some guilt after your first few noes, especially with family. Guilt after a fair no does not mean you did wrong; it is often just the discomfort of a new habit. Check your decision against your reason. If the reason is still true, the no stands. If you learn something new that changes the picture, you are free to change your mind, and saying so openly is also assertive.

Holding boundaries gets easier with practice. People who are used to your yes may be surprised at first. Keep your tone warm and your words few, and most relationships adjust. If someone responds to a respectful no with threats or harm, return to the safety guidance in Module 1.

takeaways: Every unwilling yes is a no to something else
Positive no: yes to your reason, a clear no, then an offer
Repeat calmly and agree with any truth, without changing your decision
One honest reason is enough; you may ask for time

activity.title: Prepare three positive noes
steps: List three requests you often agree to but would like to refuse or limit.
For each, write a Yes, No, Yes? answer in your own words.
Write one calm repeat sentence for each, ready for when you are pushed.
Practise all three aloud with a trusted friend playing the person who asks.
Use one in real life this week and note what happened.
activity.evidence: Three written positive-no scripts and a short note on the one you used

quiz.q: Your friend says she lost her job. Which response is a paraphrase?
options: "So after six years there, they let you go on Friday with no warning."
"My own sister lost her job too, it was worse."
quiz.explain: A paraphrase restates the speaker's main point in your words so she can confirm or correct it.

quiz.q: Which is an open question?
quiz.explain: Open questions start with what, how, which or tell me and invite a fuller answer.

quiz.q: Which sentence is an observation rather than a judgement?
quiz.explain: An observation records what a camera would see, with no interpretation such as careless or disrespectful.

quiz.q: Which statement names a real feeling rather than an accusation?
quiz.explain: Worried and tired describe your inner state. Ignored and betrayed describe what you think someone did, and "I feel that you" is a thought.

quiz.q: Kemi asks her husband to collect the children on Friday. He says no, and she sulks and refuses to speak to him all weekend. What does this show?
options: It was really a demand, because a no led to punishment
NVC does not work in marriage
quiz.explain: In NVC, how you respond to a no shows whether it was a request or a demand.

quiz.q: A neighbour keeps pressing you to buy into an investment you have already refused. Which reply uses calm repetition well?
options: A long list of your expenses
"I understand it's important to you. I'm still not putting money in."
quiz.explain: Calm repetition restates your decision in the same tone without new excuses, so there is nothing new to argue about.

quiz.q: Which is the best Yes, No, Yes? reply to a request to cook for a party on your only free day?
options: "I need Saturday to rest because I work all week, so I can't cook. I can share my jollof recipe with whoever does."
"Why do you people always disturb me?"
quiz.explain: It gives your reason (yes to rest), a clear no, and a real alternative that keeps the relationship warm.

modules.title: Quality and Evidence: Voice, Honesty and Feedback
modules.overview: Good self-expression is judged by how it lands, not only by what you meant. In this module you learn how voice and body carry your message, how to handle difficult conversations honestly and ethically, and how to give, receive and record feedback so you can prove your progress.

lessons.title: Voice, face and body: making your delivery match your words
objectives: Explain what the famous 7-38-55 figure really measured
Use pace, pauses, pitch and volume on purpose
Match your posture and face to an assertive message
Practise delivery with your phone's voice recorder

blocks.text: Two women can say the same sentence, "I need payment by Friday", and get completely different results. One looks at the floor and lets her voice fade at the end. The other stands steady, speaks at a calm pace and pauses after "Friday". This lesson is about the second woman's tools: voice, face and body, also called **nonverbal communication**.

blocks.name: mirror
blocks.caption: A mirror or your phone camera shows you what your listener sees.

blocks.text: The truth about 7-38-55

You may have heard that only 7% of communication is words, 38% is tone and 55% is body language. This comes from small experiments by the psychologist Albert Mehrabian in the 1960s. The studies looked at how people judged feelings and attitudes from single words when the tone or face disagreed with the word. Mehrabian himself has said the figures do not apply to ordinary communication. The useful lesson is narrower and true: **when your words and your delivery disagree, people believe the delivery.** If you say "I'm not angry" through clenched teeth, nobody believes the words.
Your voice toolbox

head: Tool
What it does
Try this
rows: Pace
Fast speech sounds nervous or rushed; calm speech sounds sure
Slow down for the most important sentence
Pause
Gives weight to what came before and lets people think
Pause for two seconds after your main request
Pitch
A rising pitch at the end turns a statement into a question
Let your voice go down at the end of a request
Volume
Too soft sounds unsure; too loud sounds aggressive
Speak so the farthest person can hear, no louder
Warmth
A smile in the voice makes firm words easier to accept
Smile slightly before you start a hard sentence

blocks.text: The speaker Julian Treasure, in his TED talk on speaking so that people want to listen, describes a similar toolbox (register, timbre, prosody, pace, silence, pitch and volume) and four foundations he sums up as HAIL: honesty, authenticity, integrity and love. The tools only work on top of an honest message.

blocks.title: Assertive body check
items: Feet steady, weight balanced
Shoulders relaxed, not raised
Face calm, matching the message
Hands open and still
Voice drops at the end
blocks.caption: Run this quick check just before an important sentence.

blocks.text: Face, posture and culture

Body language is partly cultural. In many Nigerian settings a younger person avoids long direct eye contact with an elder, kneels or bows when greeting, and keeps hands still. These are signs of respect, not weakness, and you can keep them. Assertiveness shows instead in a steady voice, finished sentences and a calm face. Signals that weaken you in almost any culture include nervous laughter after a serious sentence, covering your mouth while speaking, apologising before every request and letting your voice trail off.

blocks.title: Worked example: practising a payment request with a voice recorder
blocks.context: For example, Ruth, a caterer in Jos, needs to ask a client for the ₦45,000 balance on a birthday order. She records herself on her phone's voice recorder app.
steps: Recording 1: "Sorry ehn, I just wanted to ask, maybe if it's possible, about the balance?" It lasts 9 seconds, her voice rises at the end and she laughs nervously.
She removes the filler words (sorry, just, maybe, if it's possible) and writes: "Good afternoon, Mrs Bello. I'm calling about the ₦45,000 balance for the birthday order. Can you pay it by Friday?"
Recording 2: she slows down and pauses after the amount. Her voice still rises on "Friday".
Recording 3: she stands up while speaking, smiles before starting and lets her voice go down on "Friday?" so it sounds like a clear request.
She plays recordings 1 and 3 back to back to hear the difference.
blocks.result: The final version takes about 7 seconds, has no apologies or filler words and sounds calm and sure. Ruth makes the call, and the client sends the balance two days later.

blocks.title: Voice notes count too
blocks.text: Before sending an important voice note, listen to it once yourself. If you hear anger, rushing or a long ramble, delete it and record again, or send a short text instead.
Filler words and hedges

Filler words such as "ehn", "like", "you know" and "just", and hedges such as "maybe", "I think perhaps" and "if it's not a problem", make a clear request sound unsure. You do not need to remove every one, because some softness is polite. Remove them from the one sentence that carries your main point. A quick test is to write that sentence down and cross out every word the listener does not need. What remains is usually stronger and kinder, because it is easier to understand.

Practise your delivery in safe places first: reading a Bible or Quran passage aloud, telling your children a story, or making a toast at a family event. Each time, choose one tool, such as the pause, and use it on purpose.

takeaways: When words and delivery disagree, people believe the delivery
Slow down, pause and let your voice drop on requests
Respectful cultural gestures fit well with a steady voice
Record and replay yourself to hear what others hear

activity.title: Three-take voice practice
steps: Choose one real request you need to make this week.
Record it once on your phone exactly as you would naturally say it.
Write down the filler words and any rising endings you hear.
Rewrite it without filler and record it two more times, standing, with a pause after the key point.
Compare the first and last recordings and note two changes.
activity.evidence: Your first and third recordings (kept on your phone) and a note listing what changed

lessons.title: Difficult conversations with honesty and respect
objectives: Prepare for a difficult conversation using the three layers: what happened, feelings and identity
Open a hard conversation with a calm, neutral first sentence
Make a sincere apology without excuses
Apply ethical limits: no gossip, no manipulation, respect for privacy

blocks.text: A difficult conversation is any talk you dread: telling an in-law her comments hurt you, raising a money problem in a cooperative, or admitting you made a mistake. The book *Difficult Conversations* by Douglas Stone, Bruce Patton and Sheila Heen, from the Harvard Negotiation Project, points out that every hard conversation is really three conversations happening at once.

blocks.name: family
blocks.caption: The hardest conversations are often with the people closest to us.

blocks.title: Three layers of a difficult conversation
items: Identity: what this says about me
Feelings: what each of us feels
What happened: facts and intentions
blocks.caption: Most arguments stay on the bottom layer, while the real heat comes from the two layers above.

items: **What happened:** who said or did what, who is to blame. People argue here, but each person usually holds only part of the story. Replace "who is to blame" with "what did each of us contribute". Also separate intention from impact: she may not have intended to hurt you, and you were still hurt.
**Feelings:** the hurt, anger or fear underneath. Unspoken feelings leak out anyway, through tone and sarcasm, so it is usually better to name them simply, as you learned with NVC.

**Identity:** what this situation seems to say about you. "Am I a bad daughter-in-law if I complain?" "Am I a failure because the contribution is short?" Noticing this layer calms you, because you can remind yourself the conversation is about a situation, not your whole worth.

blocks.text: Opening without starting a fight

The first sentence often decides the next ten minutes. Begin from what the authors call the third story: a neutral description that an outsider watching would accept, followed by an invitation. Avoid starting with your conclusion about the other person.

head: Opening that starts a fight
Neutral opening
rows: "Mama, you are always insulting my cooking in front of people."
"Mama, can I talk with you about something that happened on Sunday? I'd like us to understand each other better."
"Treasurer, some of us are suspecting you."
"I've noticed the account balance and our records don't match by ₦12,000. Can we go through it together to find the difference?"
"You have finally shown your true colour."
"I think we see what happened at the shop differently. I'd like to hear your side, then share mine."

blocks.title: Worked example: a mother-in-law and public comments
blocks.context: For example, Chioma lives near her husband's mother in Owerri. At a family gathering her mother-in-law said loudly that Chioma's soup "has no taste". It is the third time this year. Chioma prepares using the three layers.
steps: What happened: she writes the facts (three public comments, the last on Sunday in front of guests) and admits her part: she has never said anything, so her mother-in-law may not know it hurts.
Feelings: embarrassed and hurt, and a little angry.
Identity: she notices she fears being seen as a disrespectful wife. She reminds herself that a respectful private talk is not disrespect.
She chooses a private moment on a weekday afternoon, greets properly and opens neutrally: "Mama, can I share something that has been on my mind since Sunday?"

She uses NVC: "When my soup was described as tasteless in front of the guests, I felt embarrassed. I want to learn your way of cooking. Would you be willing to tell me privately what to change, instead of in front of people?"
blocks.result: Her mother-in-law says she meant it as a joke, but agrees, and offers to show Chioma how she prepares ofe owerri. The relationship becomes warmer, not colder.

blocks.text: A sincere apology

Sometimes the difficult conversation is your apology. A sincere apology names what you did, takes responsibility without "but", acknowledges the effect, offers repair and commits to change. "I'm sorry I shared your news in the group before you were ready. That was your story to tell, and I embarrassed you. I've deleted the message, and I won't share your private matters again." Avoid "I'm sorry if you were offended", which quietly puts the problem back on the other person.

blocks.title: Ethical limits of self-expression
blocks.text: Speaking up is never a licence to gossip, shame people publicly, record or screenshot private conversations to use against someone, threaten, or twist facts to win. Keep other people's private information private, including health, money and family matters shared in confidence. Honest and respectful means both, always.

Timing matters as much as words. Avoid starting a hard talk when either person is hungry, rushed, in front of an audience or late at night. If emotions rise too high during the talk, it is fine to pause: "I want to get this right. Can we continue tomorrow after work?"

Not every difficult conversation ends in agreement. Success means you said what was true for you, listened to what was true for the other person, and left the relationship as healthy as possible. Sometimes the best result is "we see this differently, and we can still work together."

takeaways: Every hard talk has three layers: facts, feelings and identity
Separate intention from impact
Open with a neutral description and an invitation
Apologise without "but" and offer repair

activity.title: Three-layer preparation sheet
steps: Choose one difficult conversation you have been avoiding (not one where you would be unsafe).
Write what happened, including what you may have contributed.
Write the feelings on both sides and what identity question it raises for you.
Write a neutral opening sentence and one NVC request.
Decide when and where you will have the conversation.
activity.evidence: Your completed three-layer sheet with opening sentence, request and planned date

lessons.title: Giving and receiving feedback, and tracking your progress
objectives: Give feedback using Situation, Behaviour, Impact
Receive feedback by listening, thanking, clarifying and deciding
Keep a weekly communication journal
Measure progress with simple counts and repeated self-ratings

blocks.text: You cannot improve what you never check. This lesson gives you two tools for evidence: a clear way to give and receive feedback, and a simple journal that shows your progress over weeks. Both will feed directly into your final project.

blocks.name: feedback
blocks.caption: Feedback is information that helps both people improve.

blocks.text: Giving feedback with SBI

The Center for Creative Leadership teaches a feedback method called **Situation, Behaviour, Impact (SBI)**. You describe the situation (when and where), the specific behaviour you saw or heard, and its impact on you or the work. It keeps feedback factual and avoids personal attacks, and it works for praise as well as correction.

blocks.title: The SBI feedback model
items: Situation: when and where
Behaviour: what you saw
Impact: the effect
blocks.caption: Add a question at the end to hear the other person's side.

head: Vague feedback
SBI feedback
rows: "You are not serious with this job."
"At yesterday's delivery (S), the three cartons arrived at 2pm instead of 10am (B). The customer waited and nearly cancelled her order (I). What happened?"
"Well done."
"In Saturday's meeting (S), you summarised both sides before the vote (B). People calmed down and we finished early (I)."

blocks.text: Receiving feedback well

items: **Listen to the end** without defending yourself. Breathe.
**Thank the person** for telling you. It took courage, even if the delivery was poor.
**Clarify** with a question: "Can you give me an example?" (Manuel Smith called this negative inquiry; it turns vague criticism into useful detail.)
**Decide** later, calmly, what is true and useful, and what you will change. You do not have to accept all feedback, but you should consider it.

blocks.text: Some feedback will sting, especially if it is delivered badly. Separate the message from the messenger: even an unkind comment may contain one useful point. Ask yourself, "If a friend I trust said this calmly, would any part be true?" Keep that part and let the rest go. If several different people give you the same feedback, take it seriously; if only one person says it, treat it as one view to test.
Your weekly communication journal
Spend five minutes, once a week, recording real situations. Use the same columns each week so you can compare. Keep it in a notebook or a notes app on your phone.

head: Date
Situation
Style I used
What I said
Result
Score 1 to 5
rows: Mon
Customer owing ₦6,000
Assertive
"Can you pay by Wednesday?"
Paid Wednesday
Thu
Aunt asked me to host her friend
Passive
"Okay, no problem"
Lost two days of work

blocks.text: Three simple measures

items: **Asking rate:** how often you spoke up when you had the chance. Count chances and attempts each week, then divide attempts by chances.
**Self-rating:** re-score your ten-situation profile from Module 1 every four weeks, on the same scale, and compare totals.
**Outcome notes:** what changed because you spoke differently, such as money collected, a task shared at home, or an argument that stayed calm.

blocks.title: Worked example: four weeks of tracking
blocks.context: For example, Funmi (the hairdresser from Module 1) chose "asking customers for money owed" as her focus. Each week she counts how many times she asked directly and how much owed money came in.
steps: Week 1: asked 1 time out of 5 chances, collected ₦3,000.
Week 2: asked 3 times out of 5 chances, collected ₦7,500.
Week 3: asked 4 times out of 4 chances, collected ₦8,000.
Week 4: asked 5 times out of 6 chances, collected ₦6,500.
Totals: she asked 13 times out of 20 chances, which is 13 ÷ 20 = 65%. In Week 1 the rate was 1 ÷ 5 = 20%; in Week 4 it was 5 ÷ 6, about 83%. Total collected: 3,000 + 7,500 + 8,000 + 6,500 = ₦25,000.
blocks.result: Funmi has clear evidence: her asking rate rose from 20% to about 83%, and ₦25,000 of old balances came in. She also re-scores "asking for money owed" on her profile: from 2 to 4.

blocks.title: Measure what you control
blocks.text: You control whether you asked clearly; you do not control whether the other person says yes. Count your actions first, such as times you used a positive no or a paraphrase, then note outcomes separately.

Keep your journal private. It may contain other people's names and family matters, so do not post it in group chats. When you use entries as evidence for your certificate, use first names only or initials.

At the end of each month, read your journal from the start. Look for patterns: which people or situations still push you to passive or aggressive, and which skills now come easily. Ask one trusted person for SBI feedback on a real conversation. These notes become the evidence in your capstone.

takeaways: SBI: situation, behaviour, impact, then ask
Receive feedback: listen, thank, clarify, decide
A five-minute weekly journal turns practice into evidence
Count your actions first, then outcomes

activity.title: Start your journal and give SBI feedback
steps: Set up a journal page with the six columns: date, situation, style, what I said, result, score.
Record at least three real situations from the past week.
Give one person positive SBI feedback this week and note their reaction.
Ask one trusted person for feedback on how you communicated in a specific situation, and practise receiving it well.
activity.evidence: Your journal page with three entries and a note of the SBI feedback you gave and received

quiz.q: What did Mehrabian's 7-38-55 research actually show?
options: Words never matter in any conversation
When words and tone or face disagree about feelings, people trust the tone and face
Body language is 55% of every business email
quiz.explain: The figures came from narrow experiments on feelings and attitudes with conflicting signals. Mehrabian said they do not apply to all communication.

quiz.q: Ruth's voice rises at the end of "Can you pay by Friday?" and she laughs nervously. What change would most improve it?
options: Remove the laugh and let her voice go down at the end
Send a long voice note instead
quiz.explain: A falling pitch and no nervous laughter make a request sound calm and sure.

quiz.q: Which is the best neutral opening for a talk with a treasurer about a missing ₦12,000?
options: "The balance and our records differ by ₦12,000. Can we check it together?"
Posting the question in the group chat
quiz.explain: A neutral description plus an invitation to work together avoids accusation and keeps the conversation open.

quiz.q: Which is a sincere apology?
options: "I'm sorry I shared your news. It was yours to share. I've deleted it and won't do it again."
quiz.explain: It names the act, takes responsibility without "but", acknowledges the effect, repairs and commits to change.

quiz.q: Which is SBI feedback?
options: "At Monday's market (S), you priced the tins at ₦1,500 instead of ₦1,800 (B), so we lost ₦3,000 on ten tins (I)."
quiz.explain: It gives the situation, a specific behaviour and the impact, with correct arithmetic: ₦300 × 10 = ₦3,000.

quiz.q: Funmi asked 6 times out of 8 chances one week. What was her asking rate?

modules.title: Portfolio and Impact: Your Real Conversation and Your Story
modules.overview: You bring everything together. You will plan, rehearse and reflect on a real conversation, learn to introduce yourself and describe your skills with evidence, and finish with a complete certificate portfolio and a 90-day practice plan.

lessons.title: Plan, rehearse and reflect on a real conversation
objectives: Fill in a one-page conversation plan for a real situation
Rehearse with a partner using role reversal
Reflect afterwards with What, So what, Now what
Turn a passive or aggressive first draft into an assertive script

blocks.text: This lesson is the workshop for your capstone. You will take one real situation from your life, ideally your focus situation from Module 1, and prepare it the way a professional prepares an important meeting: on paper, out loud and with a review afterwards. Preparation does not make you sound rehearsed. It frees your attention to listen, because you are not searching for words.

blocks.name: thought-process
blocks.alt: A person thinking through a plan
blocks.caption: A few minutes of planning on paper can change the whole conversation.

blocks.title: Before, during and after
items: Plan on one page
Rehearse aloud
Hold the conversation
Reflect within 24 hours
blocks.caption: Each stage feeds the next, and your reflection becomes the plan for the next conversation.

blocks.text: The one-page conversation plan

head: Box
Question to answer
Keep it to
rows: Goal
What do I want to be different after this talk?
One sentence
Main point
If they remember only one thing, what is it?
One sentence
Their side
What might they feel and need? What will they say?
Two or three notes
Opening
How will I start, neutrally?
One sentence
Request
Observation, feeling, need, request
Four short lines
If they say no
My calm repeat sentence and my alternative
Two sentences
When and where
A calm, private time that suits both of us
Day, time, place

blocks.text: Rehearse with role reversal

Ask a trusted friend to help. First, she plays the other person and you practise your opening and request. Then swap: you play the other person and she says your lines. Hearing your own words from the other side shows you quickly which sentences sound like blame. Do three short rounds, each no longer than five minutes, and change one thing each time. If you have no partner, record yourself and answer your own recording as the other person would.

blocks.title: Worked example: sharing the school run
blocks.context: For example, Blessing, a nurse in Abuja, does every school drop-off and pick-up for her two children, even on her early shifts. Her husband Tunde works from home three days a week. Her first draft, written while angry: "You just sit at home doing nothing while I suffer."
steps: Goal: Tunde does the school run on his three home days.
Main point: "I need us to share the school run so I can manage my early shifts."
Their side: he may feel judged for working from home and need his work to be respected. He may say his calls start at 8am.
Opening: "Can we talk about the school mornings this evening after the children sleep? I want us to find a plan that works for both of us."

Request (NVC): "This week I was late for my 7am shift twice because of the drop-off. I feel stressed and worried about my job. I need the mornings shared. Would you be willing to do drop-off and pick-up on your three home days?"
If he says no: calm repeat, plus an alternative: "Could you do pick-up on those days, and we pay the neighbour's driver for two drop-offs a week?"
blocks.result: In rehearsal, her friend playing Tunde says "So my job is not important?" Blessing adds a line: "I know your work is real and your calls matter." In the real conversation Tunde agrees to all three pick-ups and two drop-offs. That is five of the six trips, and Blessing records it in her journal.

blocks.text: During the conversation

items: Start with your neutral opening, then stop and listen. Paraphrase before you answer.
Say your request once, clearly, then pause and let the silence work.
If you are pushed, use your calm repeat sentence or your alternative.
Close by summarising what was agreed, who does what and by when, and send a short text afterwards if it involves dates or money.

blocks.text: Reflect with What, So what, Now what

Within 24 hours, write a short reflection using three questions from a well-known reflective model by Gary Rolfe and colleagues. **What?** Describe what happened and what was said, as an observation. **So what?** What does it show about your skills, the other person and the situation? Which style did you use, and when did it change? **Now what?** What will you do next time, and what is the next step in this relationship?

blocks.title: If it went badly
blocks.text: An honest reflection on a conversation that went wrong is excellent evidence. Write what happened, where you slid into passive or aggressive, what you would change, and whether you plan to return to the topic. Learning is the goal, not a perfect result.

Your capstone also asks you to rewrite a passive or aggressive response as an assertive one. Blessing's first draft and final request above show exactly what is wanted: the original words, what made them aggressive (blame, "doing nothing", exaggeration), and the assertive version built from the four NVC steps.

takeaways: Plan on one page: goal, main point, their side, opening, request, fallback
Role reversal shows you which lines sound like blame
Reflect within 24 hours: What, So what, Now what
An honest account of a hard conversation is valid evidence

activity.title: Prepare your capstone conversation
steps: Choose a real conversation for your capstone that is safe for you to have.
Fill in all seven boxes of the one-page plan.
Write your first, unedited draft of what you would have said, then the assertive version.
Rehearse at least two rounds with role reversal, or with your phone recorder.
Fix a date and place for the conversation.
activity.evidence: Your completed one-page plan, the before-and-after scripts and a note of your rehearsal changes

lessons.title: Telling your own story: introductions, bios and showing your skills
objectives: Give a 60-second self-introduction using Present, Past, Future
Write a short written bio for WhatsApp, a programme or a job application
Describe a communication skill with evidence using STAR
Adjust your story for different listeners

blocks.text: Self-expression includes presenting yourself: at a women's meeting, a job interview, a training, a new church or mosque, or to a possible customer. Many capable women undersell themselves with "I'm just a trader" or say too much without a clear point. A simple structure lets you speak about yourself with confidence and honesty.

blocks.name: nice-to-meet-you
blocks.caption: A prepared introduction turns a nervous moment into a real connection.

blocks.text: Present, Past, Future

blocks.title: A 60-second introduction
items: Present: who I am now
Past: how I got here
Future: what I'm building
blocks.caption: End the Future part with a link to the listener or the occasion.

items: **Present:** your name and what you do now, in plain words.
**Past:** one or two facts that explain your experience, such as years in business, training or a key result.
**Future:** what you are working towards, and if it fits, what you are looking for from this group or person.

blocks.text: Spoken at a calm pace, 60 seconds is usually around 120 to 150 words. Write it, read it aloud with a timer on your phone, and trim until it fits comfortably. Prepare a 20-second version as well, for quick introductions.

blocks.title: Worked example: from "I'm just a trader" to a clear introduction
blocks.context: For example, Aisha sells fabrics in Kano and is asked to introduce herself at a women's business network. Her usual answer: "I'm Aisha, I'm just a small trader."
steps: Present: "Good afternoon. I'm Aisha Bello. I sell quality Ankara and lace fabrics from my stall in Kantin Kwari market and on WhatsApp."
Past: "I started eight years ago with one bale. Today about half my sales come from regular customers who order on WhatsApp."
Future: "This year I want to supply fabric to tailors in bulk. If you are a tailor or know one, I'd love to talk after the meeting."
She counts the words: 69 words, a little over 30 seconds aloud, leaving time to smile, pause and add one line about her delivery service if asked.
blocks.result: Aisha now has a clear, honest, specific introduction with a direct invitation at the end. Two tailors approach her after the meeting.

blocks.text: Three common mistakes

items: **Starting with an apology:** "I'm not very good at speaking, but..." Skip it and begin with your name.
**Telling your whole life story:** choose one or two facts from the past that support your future goal.
**Ending without a link:** finish with what you hope for from this group or person, or a simple "I look forward to learning with you all."

blocks.text: Adapt the language to the room. In a local association, greeting in the language most members use and then switching to English, or the reverse, can show respect and warmth. In a formal interview, keep to the language of the interview and keep Pidgin for casual moments unless it is clearly welcome.
A short written bio

You will also need written versions: a WhatsApp "About" line, a short profile for a programme brochure, or the opening paragraph of an application. Write in the first person for WhatsApp and personal messages ("I make..."), and in the third person for programmes and brochures ("Aisha Bello sells..."). Keep one fact that makes you specific, such as years of experience, a number of customers you have served, a training you finished, or a community role. Only include facts you can stand behind.

head: Where
Length
Example
rows: WhatsApp About
One line
"Fabrics for tailors and families. Kantin Kwari, Kano. Orders by WhatsApp."
Programme profile
2 to 3 sentences
"Aisha Bello has sold Ankara and lace fabrics in Kano for eight years. She now supplies tailors and is building a bulk delivery service."
Application opening
3 to 4 sentences
Present, Past, Future, plus why you are applying to this specific programme

blocks.text: Showing a skill with STAR

Saying "I am a good communicator" proves nothing. Interviewers and programme selectors look for evidence, and the **STAR** method gives it shape: Situation (the context), Task (what you had to achieve), Action (what you did, in detail) and Result (what changed). Your journal and capstone give you true STAR stories.

blocks.title: STAR from your journal
blocks.text: Situation: our cooperative's records were ₦12,000 short. Task: raise it without accusing anyone. Action: I asked the treasurer privately, used a neutral opening and suggested we check the records together. Result: we found two unrecorded withdrawals, corrected the book and agreed to have two people sign every withdrawal.

Adjust your story to the listener. A buyer wants to know what you sell and why she can trust you. An employer wants evidence of skills and reliability. A community group wants to know what you care about and how you can contribute. Same true facts, different emphasis.

takeaways: Present, Past, Future gives a clear introduction
60 seconds is roughly 120 to 150 spoken words
Use one specific, true fact to stand out
Show skills with STAR stories, not adjectives

activity.title: Write and record your introductions
steps: Write a 60-second Present, Past, Future introduction and a 20-second version.
Time yourself reading both aloud and trim until they fit.
Write a WhatsApp About line and a two-sentence third-person profile.
Write one STAR story from your journal or capstone that shows a communication skill.
activity.evidence: Your two written introductions with timings, your two bios and one STAR story

lessons.title: Your certificate portfolio and 90-day practice plan
objectives: Check your portfolio against the certificate evidence list
Re-score your communication profile and compare it with your first score
Write a 90-day practice plan with weekly actions
Choose a practice partner and your next course

blocks.text: Certification at the WODDI Institute reflects practice in real life, not only correct quiz answers. Before you take the final quiz, gather your evidence into one place: a folder on your phone, a notebook or a document. This lesson walks you through the checklist, your before-and-after comparison and a plan to keep growing for the next three months.

blocks.name: certificate
blocks.caption: Your certificate is backed by real conversations and real evidence.

blocks.text: Portfolio checklist

items: Your Module 1 communication profile with the date, total score and focus situation.
Your one-page conversation plan for a real situation (Module 4, Lesson 1).
Your before-and-after scripts: the original passive or aggressive draft, what made it so, and the assertive version.
Your What, So what, Now what reflection on how the conversation went, even if it went badly.
At least four weeks of communication journal entries with counts.
Your 60-second introduction and one STAR story.
Your 90-day plan (below).

blocks.text: Compare before and after

Re-score the same ten situations from Module 1 on the same 1 to 5 scale, without looking at your old scores first. Then compare. Do not worry if some scores stay the same or even drop; often a drop means you are now more honest with yourself. What matters is that you can explain the change with examples from your journal.

blocks.title: Worked example: reading the change
blocks.context: For example, Funmi's first profile total was 28 out of 50. After the course she scores 36 out of 50.
steps: Change in total: 36 minus 28 = 8 points.
As a percentage of her starting score: 8 ÷ 28 is about 0.29, so about 29% higher.
Biggest change: asking for money owed, from 2 to 4, backed by her journal (asking rate from 20% to about 83%, ₦25,000 collected).
No change: saying no to relatives stays at 1. She names this as the focus of her 90-day plan.
blocks.result: Funmi's portfolio shows real progress with evidence, and an honest next challenge. That honesty strengthens her portfolio rather than weakening it.

blocks.text: Your 90-day plan

blocks.title: Ninety days in three stages
items: Days 1 to 30: practise
Days 31 to 60: stretch
Days 61 to 90: review
blocks.caption: Each stage builds on the last, with the journal running through all three.

head: Stage
Focus
Weekly action
rows: Days 1 to 30
Your new focus situation in low-risk settings
Use one positive no or one NVC request a week; journal it
Days 31 to 60
The same skill with a harder person or a bigger issue
One planned conversation every two weeks using the one-page plan
Days 61 to 90
Review and share
Re-score your profile, ask for SBI feedback, and teach one skill to a friend or your group

blocks.text: Write your plan where you will see it, such as a note pinned in your phone or inside your notebook cover. Keep the weekly actions small enough to do even in a busy week. A plan of one honest request a week that you actually complete is stronger than an ambitious plan you abandon in week two. If you miss a week, restart the next week without punishing yourself; just record the gap honestly in your journal.
A practice partner

Choose one person, perhaps someone from your WODDI cohort, to check in with every two weeks for 15 minutes. Each of you shares one journal entry, and the other gives SBI feedback. Agree up front that what is shared stays private. Teaching what you have learned to someone else is also one of the best ways to make it stick.

blocks.title: Worked example: a 90-day plan in numbers
blocks.context: For example, Funmi's 90-day focus is saying no to relatives, which she scored 1. She plans one positive no a week.
steps: Days 1 to 30: about 4 weeks, so 4 planned positive noes with friends and distant relatives.
Days 31 to 60: 2 planned conversations with closer relatives, one every two weeks, using the one-page plan.
Days 61 to 90: 1 profile re-score, 1 SBI feedback request from her practice partner, and 1 short talk to her savings group on the positive no.
Total planned actions: 4 + 2 + 3 = 9 over the 90 days.
blocks.result: Funmi's plan is small enough to finish and specific enough to check. At day 90 she will know exactly how many actions she completed and whether her score of 1 has moved.

blocks.text: Where to go next

If your next challenge is speaking to a group, take the Institute's Presentation Skills course. If it is prices, pay or agreements, take Negotiation Skills. For handling strong emotions, take Emotional Intelligence for Daily Life, and for written messages at work, Business Communication. Each builds on the listening, expressing and boundary skills from this course.

blocks.title: Keep your portfolio safe
blocks.text: Your portfolio contains personal stories about real people. Store it privately, use first names or initials, and share only what you are comfortable with when you submit evidence.

takeaways: Gather all evidence in one place before the final quiz
Compare your before and after scores and explain the change
A 90-day plan in three stages keeps practice going
A practice partner and teaching others make skills stick

activity.title: Complete your portfolio
steps: Collect every item on the portfolio checklist into one folder or notebook.
Re-score your profile and calculate the change from your first total.
Write your 90-day plan with one weekly action per stage.
Ask one person to be your practice partner and set the first check-in date.
activity.evidence: Your complete portfolio, including the before-and-after profile, the 90-day plan and your partner's name and check-in date

quiz.q: In the one-page plan, what goes in the "Main point" box?
options: The one thing you want them to remember, in one sentence
A list of their past mistakes
quiz.explain: The main point is a single sentence; it keeps you focused when emotions rise.

quiz.q: Why is role reversal useful in rehearsal?
options: It lets you memorise the other person's lines
